Return Of Part III: The Portfolio

Chapter 7 Preliminary draft

The Satellite

Swing trading and growth momentum.

The satellite is a small, rule-bound slice of your money set aside for active work. It earns its place only by following written rules.

What the satellite is for

The core carries the plan. The satellite is where you practice a skill. It is small on purpose, so a bad month in it cannot damage the core. It is also where the Ladder starts: Level 2 is swing trading and growth momentum, unlocked after the foundation work of Level 1 is done.

Active work asks for attention every morning. If the morning routine and journal lapse, the satellite goes back to the core. That is the demotion rule, and it is a feature, not a punishment.

Swing trading

Swing trading (Strategy 9) means taking technical setups and holding them for days to weeks. A setup is a pattern on a chart that you have defined in advance: a pullback to a rising average, a breakout from a base, a bounce off a level. You are not trying to hold for years. You want to capture one move and get out.

Risk is high and the effort is medium to high. Charts do not explain why a stock moves. They show what buyers and sellers have done so far. That is why a swing trade needs an exit planned before the entry.

Growth momentum

Growth Momentum (Strategy 5) joins two ideas. First, the business is strong: earnings and sales growing, leadership in its field. Second, the chart agrees: the price breaks out of a base on rising volume. This is the CAN SLIM tradition from William O’Neil. Minervini’s approach shares its spirit: trend following with risk managed first.

You enter on the breakout. You exit with a stop. The fundamentals pick the stock, the chart picks the moment, and the stop limits the damage when you are wrong. Risk is medium to high and effort is high.

Value (Strategy 4) is the patient cousin. You buy businesses below what they are worth and hold for years, in the spirit of Graham’s margin of safety. Effort is high upfront and low after that. It suits the satellite’s slow end, and it needs no chart.

Every entry is written down

Before you buy, write three numbers in the journal: the entry price, the stop, and the target. No entry, no trade. If you cannot name the stop, you do not know your risk, and you are guessing.

The three numbers also give you a ratio. If the target is far above the entry and the stop is close below it, the trade pays more than it risks. If not, skip it.

Size each position so that hitting the stop costs about 1% of the satellite. A tight stop allows a larger position. A wide stop allows a smaller one. The math belongs to Chapter 10, Risk and Sizing, which covers stops, the 1% rule and expectancy.

If you cannot name the stop, you do not know your risk.

How you know it works

Feeling good about a few winners proves nothing. The journal does. After enough trades, it shows whether your setups have positive expectancy, and whether you followed your own rules. Promotion up the Ladder needs both, with at least 90% adherence.

Open questions

  • Which one or two setups will you trade first, and how exactly do you define each?
  • What share of your total portfolio is the satellite?
  • What fundamental screen picks the candidates for growth momentum?
  • What is the maximum holding period before a swing trade is reviewed?
  • Will you test Value as part of the satellite, or leave it to the core?

Further reading

  • William J. O’Neil, How to Make Money in Stocks
  • Mark Minervini, Trade Like a Stock Market Wizard
  • Benjamin Graham, The Intelligent Investor
